text:
About this site

# About vpspricewatch.com

vpspricewatch.com is an independent VPS price tracking project. It is independently maintained and does not act as an agent for any hosting provider.

## What this site does

It collects and publishes public VPS plan prices observed directly on official hosting provider pages. Every listing links back to its official source so visitors can confirm the current terms themselves.

The project does not sell hosting, does not represent any hosting provider, and never changes the prices shown by providers. Listings are price observations, not guaranteed coupons or discounts.

## Why it exists

Provider pricing pages are spread across many sites and change often. This project keeps a single, source-linked view of public plan prices so the comparison is easy to verify.

## Contact

Questions or corrections? See the [contact page](https://vpspricewatch.com/contact).

# Azure virtual server pricing: retail rates are not your account bill

Azure virtual server pricing depends on the evidence channel as well as the selected service. Public Retail Prices data provides retail rates; it does not establish your negotiated account price or actual charge. Microsoft labels non-USD catalog prices as reference values for estimates. A calculator can use selected agreement pricing, but its output remains an estimate. Our original source register makes these boundaries explicit without accessing any account or inventing a discount.

## What the official pricing documents establish

Microsoft describes Retail Prices as an unauthenticated retail-rate source. Its property table labels retailPrice as retail pricing without a discount and unitPrice as the same value. It treats non-USD values as references for estimates. The calculator documentation explains retail estimates and how selected billing accounts, profiles or agreements can supply negotiated pricing. Neither a public rate nor a calculator estimate is presented here as a private invoice.

## Our original source-first register

We place the evidence source ahead of any account label. The register holds currency, whether an agreement is linked, whether the account matches and whether a required profile is selected. These are explicit synthetic metadata fields, not details extracted from your browser. A source category cannot be changed simply by adding an account-looking annotation. The register does not store a quoted amount, so it cannot output an invented discount or a supposed invoice total. Its only output is the supported interpretation of the supplied evidence fields.

## Six reproducible evidence cases

All inputs below are project-selected synthetic metadata, not real sessions, prices or billing profiles.

| Case | Evidence description | Register output | 
| A | {'source': 'retail_catalog', 'currency': 'USD'} | public USD retail rate | 
| B | {'source': 'retail_catalog', 'currency': 'EUR'} | non-USD reference rate | 
| C | {'source': 'calculator', 'agreement_linked': False} | retail estimate, not invoice | 
| D | {'source': 'calculator', 'agreement_linked': None} | unresolved agreement scope | 
| E | {'source': 'calculator', 'agreement_linked': True, 'account_matches': True, 'profile_selected': True} | agreement-linked estimate, not invoice | 
| F | {'source': 'calculator', 'agreement_linked': True, 'account_matches': False, 'profile_selected': True} | different account scope | 

[Download inputs, classification rule and source hashes](audit-inputs.json) · [Run the original checker](audit-checker.py)

## Cases A and B: currency does not add account evidence

Our first pair uses the same public-catalog source and changes only a currency code, from USD to EUR. Case A returns public USD retail rate; case B returns non-USD reference rate. Both remain public evidence. The currency change cannot supply an agreement, selected account or paid transaction. We also remove the currency in a separate test, which produces an unresolved currency result. No exchange rate or converted amount is calculated. This pair tests the boundaries of a label rather than the cost of any Azure VM.

## Cases C and D: unknown is different from explicitly retail

Case C represents a synthetic calculator record whose agreement flag is explicitly false. Its output is retail estimate, not invoice. Case D leaves that flag unknown, and the result stays unresolved agreement scope. These are different records even though neither includes account pricing evidence. Our method preserves the difference between a verified absence of a linked agreement and information that was never checked. A screenshot of a large total cannot fill this missing flag. The test does not read a live calculator or infer a contract from a login avatar.

## Case E: a linked agreement still does not create a bill

We next set the synthetic agreement-linked flag true, the account-match flag true and the profile-selected flag true. The output is agreement-linked estimate, not invoice. This result records the evidence chain without promoting anticipated usage into observed consumption. No private billing profile was opened, and no price sheet was downloaded for this example. The fixture is a control that protects the estimate qualifier when more account-scope evidence is present. It does not promise a discount, identify its amount or say that your account has an agreement.

## Case F and the annotation control

Case F changes only the account-match flag to false while retaining the linked agreement and selected profile. The checker returns different account scope. In an additional control, we attach an agreement-looking flag to a public USD catalog record; the output remains public USD retail rate because its source has not changed. We also reject a text value in place of an explicit agreement flag and keep unsupported sources separate. These tests prevent an attractive annotation from overriding provenance. They are synthetic input checks, not observed account errors.

## Do equal retailPrice and unitPrice values prove there is no account discount?

No. The public API documentation defines these public fields as equal. That equality does not inspect your private agreement. Keep public field definitions separate from the pricing evidence for the selected billing account. Our register deliberately avoids calculating a discount from public field names.

## What this audit leaves unknown

This page supplies no live Azure rate, customer contract, invoice amount or actual usage. It does not query the Retail Prices API or sign in to the calculator. The classification is a partial evidence model, not a full Azure pricing or billing implementation. Service parameters and applicable account documentation still need to be established before an account-specific conclusion.

# Azure VM pricing: keep savings-plan hours separate

Azure VM pricing has no single universal savings-plan price. A discounted compute rate comes with an hourly spending commitment: unused commitment expires within that hour, while eligible usage beyond it is billed at pay-as-you-go rates. Check hourly utilisation before treating the discounted rate as your effective cost. Our isolated synthetic examples show the boundary; they are not Azure quotes, real bills or a recommendation to buy a commitment.

## The official hourly boundary

Microsoft documents a fixed hourly commitment and automatic allocation to eligible usage within its scope. The compute plan does not cover software, storage or networking charges. Unused hourly commitment does not carry forward. Its allocation documentation applies benefits to higher-discount eligible usage first and bills subsequent usage at pay-as-you-go rates when commitment is exhausted. This article isolates one meter rather than reproducing all allocation priorities.

## Our original isolated-hour worksheet

We separate a commitment field from a discounted rate field, even though both may appear beside a price offer. The first is a spending amount for each hour; the second prices a unit of eligible usage. Our worksheet adds usage and an on-demand rate, then carries the hour identifier through every result. We chose all numerical inputs ourselves in fictional currency units. They are not scraped Azure rates. The worksheet excludes taxes, other meters, negotiated contracts and reservations, and it cannot forecast a customer bill.

## Inputs and reproducible formulas

All numeric inputs below are synthetic constants chosen for this worksheet. Official sources establish the rule, not these prices. No server was rented.

Covered units = min(usage, commitment / savings rate). Excess = usage − covered units. Unused commitment = commitment − covered units × savings rate. Model cost = commitment + excess × pay-as-you-go rate. Baseline = usage × pay-as-you-go rate.

| Hour case | Commitment | Usage | Savings rate | Paygo rate | Model cost | Unused | 
| A | 2 | 1 | 1 | 2 | 2 | 1 | 
| B | 2 | 3 | 1 | 2 | 4 | 0 | 
| C | 2 | 2 | 1 | 2 | 2 | 0 | 
| D | 2 | 0 | 1 | 2 | 2 | 2 | 
| E | 2 | 3 | 0.5 | 2 | 2 | 0.5 | 

[Download all inputs, formulas and source hashes](audit-inputs.json) · [Run the original checker](audit-checker.py)

## Case A: a lower rate can leave commitment unused

Our first fictional hour sets commitment to two, usage to one, the savings rate to one and the on-demand rate to two. The covered quantity is min of one and two divided by one, which is one. One unit of commitment remains unused, but the model cost remains two. The on-demand-only baseline is also two. In this constructed hour a lower unit rate produces no reduction in the final isolated total. This is an arithmetic counterexample, not a statement about an actual VM size or customer.

## Case B: the next hour does not inherit the leftover

We reuse the same chosen rates and commitment but set usage to three. The model covers two units and leaves one excess unit. The result is two plus one times two, or four. Case A left one unit of commitment unused, yet that field is not passed into case B. Preserving this boundary is the purpose of our regression test. A model that adds the previous leftover would change the allocation mechanism. We do not infer that your account has either usage pattern.

## Two independent hours versus one pooled calculation

Adding our actual model outputs for cases A and B produces two plus four, or six. An intentionally incorrect pooled control combines commitment into four and usage into four, keeping both rates unchanged. It returns four because it implicitly lets the earlier unused unit cover later usage. The two-unit difference comes entirely from this pooling assumption. Our checker asserts both results to make the error reproducible. These fictional currency totals describe a test, not an estimate of your spending or a measured saving.

## Cases C and D: full use and an empty hour

Case C sets usage to two, exactly filling our commitment at the chosen savings rate. Its model cost is two against a fictional on-demand baseline of four. Case D changes usage to zero: the commitment is wholly unused, and the model still returns two while the baseline becomes zero. Keeping these two extremes next to the same rate prevents an average discount label from hiding different utilisation outcomes. We have not averaged them into a promised monthly percentage or assumed that either pattern occurs on your site.

## Case E: hold the commitment fixed when testing a rate

Our final fixture changes the selected savings rate to one half, leaving commitment at two and usage at three. Covered usage consumes one and one half units of commitment, so one half remains unused. The total model cost stays two. This test checks that the implementation deducts a discounted usage amount from the commitment rather than treating commitment as a fixed number of VM units. The numbers remain invented test constants. They must not be presented as an Azure sale, advertised discount or actual account quote.

## Can a monthly average replace the hourly rows?

Not in this model. The paired-hour control shows why averaging away the boundary can hide expired commitment. Keep each hour separate. For a real Azure account, the documented eligibility and allocation rules, including other benefits, must also be considered; this checker is not a full billing implementation.

## What this page cannot establish

No plan was bought, no account usage was read, and no rate was verified for a selected region or VM. Microsoft also documents more complex benefit allocation and reporting behaviour than this isolated model covers. The examples do not decide which commitment you should purchase. They explain one pricing boundary and leave actual contractual and usage inputs unknown.

## Official evidence and test provenance

Captured October 11, 2026. Numerical examples are project-authored synthetic fixtures, not official rates.

title: Best VPS server: compare CPU allocation before counting cores
text:
# Best VPS server: compare CPU allocation before counting cores

The best VPS server depends on the workload and the access its quote actually includes. Start by separating shared from dedicated CPU allocation; identical vCPU counts do not establish identical sustained throughput. DigitalOcean documents these as different access arrangements. Our original comparison register keeps allocation, region, family and generation visible, and leaves missing fields unknown. It checks labels, not performance, and produces no provider ranking.

## What the documented CPU labels mean

DigitalOcean describes dedicated CPU Droplets as having guaranteed access to a full hyper-thread. A shared CPU Droplet may share that thread with other Droplets, so full access is not guaranteed. Those provider-specific descriptions establish an allocation distinction. They do not supply a measured speed ratio between arbitrary plans. Keep the plan family and applicable generation alongside a vCPU count rather than borrowing a definition from a different provider.

## Our original quote-field register

We created seven required columns: provider, product, region, plan family, vCPU count, allocation and generation. The comparison checks which columns are missing before marking differences between known values. It never fills a blank allocation cell from a low price or a premium marketing word. All records in our test suite use fictional provider and family names so that no row looks like a purchasable offer. The register is a way to preserve scope when reading a quote, not a shopping score or a CPU benchmark.

## Six reproducible synthetic comparisons

All names, counts and changed values in this table are invented test inputs. They are not official plan specifications or measured server results. The left reference has two vCPUs and a shared allocation label.

| Case | Changed right-record fields | Result | 
| A | allocation: dedicated | different quote fields | 
| B | allocation: None | unknown fields | 
| C | none | matching labels, performance untested | 
| D | vcpu_count: 4 | different quote fields | 
| E | generation: None | unknown fields | 
| F | provider: other-synthetic-provider, region: other-test-region | different quote fields | 

[Download all records, formulas and capture hashes](audit-inputs.json) · [Run the original comparison checker](audit-checker.py)

## Case A: isolate allocation while keeping the count fixed

The reference and comparison both have two fictional vCPUs. We change only the allocation label from shared to dedicated, leaving provider, region, family and generation unchanged. The checker returns a difference in allocation. That result does not assign a numerical performance improvement or declare the dedicated-labelled record best. It merely shows why a count-only comparison would discard an input that the quote register treats as material. A swapped-record test finds the same changed field, so the result does not depend on which row was presented first.

## Case B: an omitted field cannot become a cheap equivalent

Our next record keeps the same count but replaces allocation with an unknown value. The checker lists allocation as missing. It does not infer shared allocation from cost, and it does not assume dedicated allocation because a plan name sounds premium. The fixture contains no price at all. This intentional omission is useful when checking whether a comparison table has enough evidence to compare entitlements. Restore the documented allocation field before treating the row as matched; do not generate a convenient value to complete the table.

## Case C: matching all labels still leaves performance untested

For the third pair we change nothing. Every required label matches, and the checker returns matching labels, performance untested. This result is deliberately narrower than same speed or best value. No latency, throughput, CPU model sample, host contention or workload measurement is present in either record. Matching published fields can be a prerequisite for a fair comparison without being its final result. Our fixture protects that boundary by requiring the untested qualifier even when the register has no missing cells or differences.

## Cases D and E: more units and an unknown generation

Case D changes the fictional count from two to four while preserving allocation. The output records a count difference and stops short of promising double throughput. Case E leaves the count at two but removes generation; the output is an unknown field. In our method a larger count and a missing generation are different evidence problems, so they cannot be summarized by one winner badge. We have not divided a price by either count, estimated a workload result or assumed a hardware generation from a provider name.

## Case F and the malformed-input controls

The final pair changes both fictional provider and region. The checker reports those two scope differences while leaving the equal CPU fields intact. We also supplied zero, a negative value, a boolean and a fractional CPU count; each was rejected by our positive-integer fixture model. This input rule describes the synthetic register, not every possible cloud configuration sold by a provider. It prevents our own test rows from quietly becoming a comparison of invalid values. No server was provisioned, and no external account was queried.

## Does dedicated CPU automatically identify the best VPS server?

No. An allocation label describes an access arrangement; it cannot settle your workload requirements, the rest of the quote or measured performance. The official plan guide discusses workload fit. This page therefore gives a comparison method rather than claiming a universal winner.

## What remains unmeasured

This documentation-based register does not contain current offer prices, purchased servers or benchmark results. It does not rank providers or predict workload capacity. The fictional records explain how our field checks work; they do not describe actual DigitalOcean plans. Other providers require their own applicable definitions and source evidence.

## Official evidence and test provenance

Captured October 13, 2026. All comparison records are project-authored synthetic fixtures.

title: Did that cheap VPS price change, or was the page just refreshed?
text:
# Did that cheap VPS price change, or was the page just refreshed?

Compare two dated records of the same plan, currency and billing basis, not the date printed on a comparison article. Our saved cheap VPS observations show four Hostinger plans with unchanged recorded prices between October 5 and October 7, 2026. That does not prove the provider kept the price unchanged throughout the interval, and it is not a current checkout quote.

## Saved observation pairs

| Plan | First USD | Second USD | Recorded delta USD | 
| KVM 1 | 6.49 | 6.49 | 0.00 | 
| KVM 2 | 8.99 | 8.99 | 0.00 | 
| KVM 4 | 12.99 | 12.99 | 0.00 | 
| KVM 8 | 25.99 | 25.99 | 0.00 | 

[Download input ledger, timestamps and hashes](observations.json)

## What our saved records actually show

Our two retained datasets record KVM 1 at USD 6.49, KVM 2 at USD 8.99, KVM 4 at USD 12.99 and KVM 8 at USD 25.99, each labelled monthly in the stored records. The first dataset carries the UTC observation time 2026-10-05T06:47:28Z; the second carries 2026-10-07T00:46:55Z. Each pair points to the same official Hostinger VPS page. We extracted these values from our repository history, rather than reconstructing an earlier price from today’s page. The downloadable ledger preserves the two revision identifiers and input hashes so this comparison can be reproduced.

## A timestamp change is not a price change

For KVM 1 the recorded difference is 6.49 minus 6.49, or USD 0.00. The corresponding subtractions are 8.99 minus 8.99 for KVM 2, 12.99 minus 12.99 for KVM 4 and 25.99 minus 25.99 for KVM 8; every recorded difference is zero. The second observation is 151167 seconds after the first: 41 hours, 59 minutes and 27 seconds. Those inputs establish a refreshed observation timestamp without an observed price-field change in these four matched rows. They do not establish a discount, a price freeze, or a continuous monitoring record. A refreshed timestamp does not produce a percentage saving figure on this page.

## The comparison refuses incompatible rows

Our reproducible comparison joins records using provider, plan title, currency, billing-period label and official source URL. We tested a currency mismatch by changing one input to EUR: it no longer matches the USD row. We also tested a billing-period mismatch by changing month to year: that row is rejected instead of being subtracted. With the unchanged KVM 1 pair, the accepted subtraction returns zero. These are deterministic software checks against saved observations; the mismatch examples are synthetic test fixtures, not additional provider offers. A missing matched row must remain unpaired, rather than becoming a zero-price offer.

## What this evidence cannot establish

The parser records a price and a monthly label; it does not preserve all configuration, commitment, renewal, tax or checkout conditions. A matched key therefore establishes comparability only within the saved fields. A provider could change an unrecorded condition while leaving the price unchanged. We have not ordered these plans, obtained a customer-specific quote, or tested a server. Confirm the current official terms before buying.

## Does an unchanged recorded price mean the cheapest offer is still available?

No. These observations do not establish availability or a market-wide cheapest ranking. Use them as evidence of what this site recorded at two particular times. If you need a buying decision, obtain the current offer and its commitment terms from the provider; do not treat our dated ledger as a guaranteed promotion.

## Evidence source

[Official Hostinger VPS page named in the saved records](https://www.hostinger.com/vps-hosting). The linked ledger is our retained observation data, not a newly collected checkout quote.

title: Cheap Windows VPS: check the RDP access path in the quote
text:
# Cheap Windows VPS: check the RDP access path in the quote

A cheap Windows VPS quote should identify how you will reach Remote Desktop, not just the VM price. In the Azure example, direct public RDP and a Bastion route have different prerequisites and quote scope. Bastion can reach a VM by private IP, but its tier, client method and availability matter. Developer is a free, limited tier; that does not make the VM or every access resource free. Our original screen records the chosen path without deploying a server or promising a final bill.

## The official route and tier boundaries

Microsoft documents a public-IP RDP path requiring a running VM and permitted TCP access from the connecting computer. Its Bastion overview describes private-IP access to the target VM. Developer uses free shared infrastructure in selected regions; browser access is available across tiers, while native-client access belongs to Standard and Premium. The overview separately describes Bastion pricing scope. These Azure-specific rules are not promises about every Windows VPS provider.

## Our original route-and-quote register

We record the provider and access route before inspecting the selected fields. A direct-public record keeps VM state, target public IP and source-specific RDP permission separate. A Bastion record keeps tier, client method, Developer availability and gateway inclusion separate. Unknown is an explicit value, not a substitute for free. The output is a limited evidence label rather than an instruction to change firewall settings. All supplied records are fictional combinations of flags; the screen has no account credentials, network scanner or deployment command.

## Eight reproducible synthetic cases

Every input below is a project-selected synthetic flag or tier selection. No connection, regional availability, checkout or invoice was tested.

| Case | Selected scope | Screen result | 
| A | direct_public / prerequisite flags | public route fields recorded; connection and price untested | 
| B | direct_public / prerequisite flags | no target public IP for this route | 
| C | direct_public / prerequisite flags | public route evidence incomplete | 
| D | bastion / Developer / browser | free Developer tier scope; other resource costs unknown | 
| E | bastion / Developer / native | native client feature mismatch | 
| F | bastion / Developer / browser | Developer availability unconfirmed | 
| G | bastion / Standard / browser | priced gateway scope missing from quote | 
| H | bastion / Standard / native | gateway quote scope recorded; actual total uncomputed | 

[Download all flags, rules and source hashes](audit-inputs.json) · [Run the original screen](audit-checker.py)

## Cases A and B: missing a public endpoint changes this route

Case A supplies a running VM, a target public-IP flag and a source-permission flag. The result says that public route fields are recorded, with connection and price untested. Case B changes only the public-IP flag to false and returns no target public IP for this route. That output does not say the VM can never be reached through a private network or another service. It says the explicitly chosen public route lacks its endpoint evidence. Neither record contains an IP charge or a purchased server.

## Case C: an unknown permission cannot prove a usable package

The next synthetic record leaves the RDP source-permission field unknown while retaining the running-state and public-IP flags. Our screen returns public route evidence incomplete. It does not fill the field from a downloaded connection file, an installed Windows image or an attractive monthly quote. This distinguishes a missing fact from an observed failed login. No login was attempted and no port was opened. The record simply identifies which prerequisite evidence is absent before anyone assumes that the advertised package meets the intended access path.

## Cases D and E: keep a free tier attached to its features

Case D selects a browser-based Developer route and explicitly supplies a positive availability flag. Its output preserves the free Developer tier scope while leaving other resource costs unknown. Case E changes only the client method to native and returns a feature mismatch. This pair prevents the free-tier label from silently inheriting an access method from another tier. Availability is a synthetic fixture input, not something we verified for a region or subscription. We have not deployed this tier or used its free label to calculate a zero total.

## Cases F and G: availability and quote inclusion are different unknowns

Case F removes the Developer availability evidence and stays unconfirmed. Case G instead selects Standard and marks its gateway scope absent from the quote. The output asks for the priced gateway scope rather than inventing an hourly amount. These cases expose different missing evidence: whether the chosen tier is available, and whether a required service has been accounted for in the quote. A low VM headline price cannot repair either omission. The method records the gap without adding an estimated fee or assuming that the package includes it.

## Case H: a recorded gateway still does not establish the final total

Our final record selects Standard with native client scope and an explicit gateway-in-quote flag. The result keeps the actual total uncomputed even though those selected fields are recorded. We also test a different provider and keep it outside this Azure-specific model, rather than carrying the same rules across brands. A text value pretending to be a verified boolean is rejected. These controls protect the evidence register itself. They do not prove successful authentication, current service availability, a security posture or an observed invoice amount.

## Does a private target IP prove that the access path is included for free?

No. It identifies the endpoint scope, not the commercial scope of the route. The Bastion guide separates tier features and pricing information. Preserve the actual access method and selected tier when checking a quote; do not infer an included gateway from the absence of a public IP on the target VM.

## What remains outside this screen

This page does not provide OS licensing advice or repeat a licence-inclusion audit. It supplies no live price, tested RDP session, created gateway or customer bill. It models only selected route, tier and quote fields from public Azure documentation. Other providers and private-network arrangements need their own applicable evidence.

## Official evidence and test provenance

Captured October 15, 2026. All route records are synthetic flags.

title: How should you compare VPS prices with different billing terms?
text:
# How should you compare VPS prices with different billing terms?

Compare the money due for the same service period, then show the payment due today separately. Record the billing term, renewal rate, included resources, and unavoidable extras before treating two advertised monthly rates as comparable. The worksheet below calculates an explicitly chosen ownership period; it does not predict your bill or select a hosting provider.

## Your billing worksheet

Enter documented amounts in one currency. Empty inputs remain unknown. This is a service-period calculation, not a checkout quote.

Comparison horizon (whole months)Introductory term (whole months)Introductory monthly equivalentRenewal monthly equivalentRequired recurring extras per monthOne-time setup chargeRequired upfront paymentCalculate from these inputs

Formula: min(H,T) × intro + max(0,H−T) × renewal + H × extras + setup. Monthly equivalent = service total ÷ H. Cash due now = entered upfront payment + setup; taxes and unentered charges remain outside this calculation.

Original worksheet diagram.

## What the provider pages establish

OVHcloud separates its VPS configurations from optional services on its public VPS page. DigitalOcean separates Droplet pricing and backup options on its public pricing page. These are useful inputs, but a product page does not establish your final checkout total. Follow the linked official sources and record the exact offer you intend to buy. This guide deliberately publishes no unverified provider price.

## Our original worksheet: keep two totals

Use two totals because they answer different questions. Service-period cost answers how much of the selected period you pay for. Cash due now answers how much money must leave your account when you order. A prepaid contract can make the first number look smaller while making the second larger. Our worksheet keeps those fields separate, so the headline result cannot hide the initial payment. It accepts your own observed inputs and makes no claim that an introductory rate is available to you.

## Record inputs before doing arithmetic

Choose a whole number of months as the comparison horizon. Record the introductory monthly equivalent, the number of months to which it applies, and the renewal monthly equivalent. Separately record any required upfront payment, recurring extras, and one-time setup charge. Copy the source URL, observation date, region, currency, and tax treatment into your notes. If a required field is unknown, leave the comparison incomplete. Do not enter zero to disguise a missing renewal rate. Zero is appropriate only when the relevant charge is confirmed to be absent.

## The calculation we implemented

Introductory months equal the smaller of the chosen horizon and the introductory term. Renewal months equal the horizon minus introductory months. Base service cost equals introductory months multiplied by the introductory monthly equivalent, plus renewal months multiplied by the renewal monthly equivalent. Add the recurring extras multiplied by the horizon and the one-time setup charge. Divide that total by the horizon to obtain the service-period monthly equivalent. These are arithmetic transformations of your inputs, not estimates of taxes, usage, exchange rates, or future provider pricing.

## Handle prepaid contracts without pretending they are monthly

Enter the quoted upfront payment separately. The service-period calculation apportions the rates across the chosen months, but it does not promise that the provider will sell that shorter term or refund an unused balance. If the order requires a longer commitment than your horizon, show the entire required payment in the cash-due-now field. Read the cancellation conditions before using an apportioned rate to make a purchase decision. This distinction is part of our worksheet design rather than a statement about any particular provider contract.

## What we tested, and what we did not

We ran the calculation locally with explicit test fixtures. In the first fixture, the horizon is 12 months, the introductory term is 3 months, the introductory rate is 5, the renewal rate is 8, recurring extras are 2 per month, and setup costs 10. The computed service total is 121 and the monthly equivalent is 121 divided by 12. In the second fixture, the horizon is 6 months and the introductory term is 12 months at a rate of 4, with no extras or setup charge; the computed service total is 24. These fixtures use arbitrary unit amounts created for software verification. They are not provider quotes, currencies, discounts, or observed hosting bills.

## Turn the worksheet into a fair comparison

Before comparing the calculated totals, compare the scope of the two offers. Write down memory, storage type and capacity, CPU allocation, region, included transfer, backup retention, and any software licence you need. Mark each required feature as included, separately priced, unavailable, or unknown. A lower total for an offer missing a required feature does not answer the same buying question. Keep the original offer URL alongside each row so that someone else can reproduce the comparison rather than trusting a screenshot of a large headline price.

## Does this tell me which VPS is cheapest?

No. It gives an auditable calculation for the offers and requirements you enter. A cheapest-provider claim would require a defined market, current comparable offers, complete fees, and a reproducible selection rule. This page has not conducted that market survey. Use the worksheet to identify missing inputs and compare documented totals within your chosen scope.

## What if the renewal price is not published?

Keep the renewal field unknown and obtain a written quote before completing a horizon that extends beyond the introductory term. A shorter horizon can describe the known period, but it does not resolve the cost of renewing. Preserve that limitation in your notes. The calculator rejects empty rate fields so an unknown charge cannot silently become a free service.

## Sources and method

Official pages fetched on 2026-10-05. Price figures are intentionally not republished.

- [OVHcloud VPS configurations and options](https://us.ovhcloud.com/vps/)
- [DigitalOcean Droplet pricing and backups](https://www.digitalocean.com/pricing/droplets)

The worksheet, comparison workflow, and fixtures were created and tested for VPS Price Watch. Fixture amounts are software test inputs.

title: Hostinger VPS pricing: check the refund clocks
text:
# Hostinger VPS pricing: check the refund clocks

Hostinger VPS pricing should not be treated as the cost of an unconditional free trial. The current refund policy adds a repeat-refund timing condition to the transaction window, and excludes VPS upgrades. Its policy and help summary describe different starting events for the repeat-refund clock. Keep transaction, prior request initiation and prior refund completion separate; a document-based timing screen cannot promise approval or a cash refund.

## What the official documents actually establish

The English policy requires a VPS refund request within 30 days of the relevant transaction and, if there was another VPS refund, more than 180 days since its initiation. The help summary instead describes 180 days from completion of the previous refund and identifies the policy as authoritative. Both exclude KVM VPS upgrades. Those different event descriptions are preserved here rather than silently replaced with one date. Purchases made using cryptocurrencies are also excluded.

## Our original document-clock register

We built a small evidence register with product, upgrade status, payment category, current transaction age, prior refund history and two prior-event ages. Each record carries an explicit unknown value when an event is missing. This avoids using a server creation date as an invoice date or using a completed payment event as the start of a prior refund request. The model checks whether two documented timing descriptions lead to the same screen result. It does not connect to a customer account or submit anything.

## Reproduce the timing fixtures

All day values below are invented test inputs, not account observations. The rule thresholds 30 and 180 come from the linked official documents. No purchase or refund was tested.

| Case | Transaction age | Prior initiation age | Prior completion age | Result | 
| A | 10 | not applicable | not applicable | screen_pass_not_approval | 
| B | 10 | 181 | 179 | document_clock_disagreement_review | 
| C | 10 | 180 | 180 | document_clock_disagreement_review | 
| D | 10 | 181 | 181 | screen_pass_not_approval | 
| E | 31 | not applicable | not applicable | outside_transaction_window | 
| F | 30 | not applicable | not applicable | transaction_boundary_review | 
| G | 10 | 181 | None | unresolved_prior_clocks | 
| H | 10 | not applicable | not applicable | excluded_upgrade | 

[Download all inputs, thresholds, formulas and capture hashes](audit-inputs.json) · [Run the original checker](audit-checker.py)

## Case A: no prior refund is an input, not a guess

Our first fixture selects a KVM VPS purchase, a non-crypto payment, no upgrade and a transaction age of ten days. It explicitly records no prior refund. The result is screen pass, not approval. That wording matters: it means only the limited known fields did not trigger a modeled rejection. It cannot establish service compliance, refund destination, paid amount or provider acceptance. In an actual private record, absence of a visible refund entry must not automatically become proof that no prior refund exists.

## Case B: two dates can cross different sides of the threshold

We selected a prior request initiation age of 181 days and a completion age of 179 days, with the current transaction ten days old. Our legal-text timing flag is true because 181 is greater than 180. Our summary timing flag is false because 179 is less than 180. The output is document clock disagreement review. We keep both inputs and both comparisons visible instead of selecting the cheaper-looking interpretation. These elapsed ages are a synthetic pair, not dates taken from a buyer or a test refund.

## Case C: the exact threshold is tested separately

For a second comparison fixture, both prior-event ages are set to 180. The literal greater-than comparison is false, while the summary-style at-least comparison is true. Our output again requests review. This test intentionally exposes the edge rather than using a rounded elapsed-month label. An actual event near a threshold needs exact timestamps and the applicable provider interpretation; our invented whole-day value does not decide the account outcome. The test is useful because changing either comparison operator would otherwise hide a meaningful implementation choice.

## Case D and the two transaction-window controls

Case D moves both prior-event ages to 181 and both limited timing flags agree. It still returns screen pass, not approval. Case E changes the current transaction age to 31 and returns outside transaction window. Case F selects an exact age of 30 and returns transaction boundary review. We deliberately avoid promising a policy cutoff instant from a rounded day value. Together these fixtures separate the prior-history clock from the current transaction clock; extending one must not reset or repair the other in our register.

## Cases G and H: missing history and a different purchase category

Case G keeps the selected prior initiation age at 181 but removes the completion age. The result stays unresolved prior clocks rather than inventing a completion date. Case H changes the upgrade field to true and receives excluded upgrade. The transaction date alone therefore cannot make the two modeled records equivalent. We also supplied a reversed chronology, where completion was older than initiation, and the checker rejected it. A different product was kept outside scope. These are input-integrity tests, not claims about a buyer eligibility.

## Does passing this screen establish the money returned?

No. It does not calculate a refund amount or identify a destination. The help summary says a processed balance refund cannot be transferred to another payment source and that some methods need alternative procedures. Keep eligibility screening separate from cash recovery. We have not inspected an invoice, requested a refund or received money.

## What remains unknown

This is a dated documentation comparison and a partial original evidence screen. It does not model every exclusion, account action, jurisdiction or provider decision. It supplies no live purchase price and does not predict a refund. Preserve the source version and exact private account events before drawing an account-specific conclusion.

## Official evidence and test provenance

Captured October 12, 2026. All elapsed ages are project-authored synthetic inputs.

# How do VPS prices change when you need seven days of backups?

Compare the server charge plus the backup option that actually meets your retention requirement. A backup taken every day but kept for only one day does not provide seven days of recovery history. Check capture frequency, retention, covered storage, and the billing basis before comparing the combined price. The matrix below keeps those requirements separate.

## Original requirement matrix

| Candidate | Capture / retention | Daily points across seven days? | Cost input | 
| DO daily percentage option | Daily / 7 days; 7 backups | Documented schedule fits; actual restore untested | D + D × 0.30 | 
| DO weekly percentage option | Weekly / 4 weeks; 4 backups | Fails a daily-capture requirement | D + D × 0.20; different scope of time | 
| OVH included automatic option | Daily / 24 hours | Fails seven-day history | Included backup; order total unknown here | 
| OVH separate automatic option | Daily / 7 rolling days | Documented schedule fits; actual restore untested | D + actual quoted F; obtain order-specific quote | 

Coverage of your attached storage and database recovery state must be checked separately for every row. No row is a tested restoration result.

Original documentation-check workflow.

## What the official pages say today

On October 6, 2026, the DigitalOcean backup pricing page lists its percentage-based daily option with seven backups, seven-day retention, and a charge of 30% of Droplet cost. Its weekly option lists four backups, four-week retention, and 20%. The OVHcloud US options page describes an included daily backup retained for 24 hours and a separate daily option retained for seven rolling days. Its advertised starting price is not a quote for your selected configuration. Verify your actual order. Both pages are linked below.

## Our original requirement matrix

We designed the matrix as a sequence of gates rather than a cheapest-price ranking. First write the oldest recovery point you need. Next write the longest acceptable gap between captures. Then list everything that must be recoverable: the system disk, separately attached volumes, and database state. Finally record the billing basis and the source date. A candidate must pass each gate before its cost is compared. This prevents long retention from concealing infrequent captures, and prevents a low backup charge from concealing storage outside its scope.

## Retention and frequency answer different questions

Use the first gate to reject a one-day history when your stated requirement is seven days. Use the second to reject weekly capture if your requirement is a recovery point from every day. Weekly capture with a longer retention period can pass the history gate while failing the daily-capture gate. This is the reasoning implemented in our comparison matrix, not a claim that one schedule is suitable for every workload. Write your own requirement first; changing the requirement after seeing the cheapest result changes the comparison.

## Treat missing scope evidence as unknown

Our matrix records storage scope separately from frequency and retention. If the public page does not establish whether an attached volume is covered, mark that cell unknown and obtain the relevant documentation before completing the comparison. Do not convert unknown into included. A database that can be copied is not automatically proven to be recoverable to your required state. This article has not bought a server, created a backup, or tested a restore. The matrix is an original documentation check; it is not experimental proof of recovery reliability.

## Calculate only after the requirements match

For a documented percentage-based option, let D be the applicable server cost for the billing period and p the published backup fraction. Backup charge B equals D multiplied by p, and the combined server-and-backup amount equals D plus B. Record what the provider means by the applicable cost before choosing D. Keep taxes, required storage charges, and unrelated extras in separate fields until their treatment is established. For a separately quoted fixed backup charge F, the corresponding arithmetic is D plus F. Neither formula supplies missing order-specific inputs.

## A reproducible calculation check

We tested the arithmetic with deliberately fictional inputs. With a server cost of 10 test units and a backup fraction of 0.30, the backup charge is 3 and the combined amount is 13. With the same fictional server cost and a separately quoted backup charge of 2 test units, the combined amount is 12. These are software fixtures, not provider prices or observed invoices. The lower fixture total does not select a winner: its retention, frequency, and scope still need to pass the same gates. Our test also rejects a missing cost rather than turning it into zero.

## Does seven-day retention mean seven daily recovery points?

Not by itself. In our matrix, the retention cell records how far back the history extends, while the frequency cell records how often points are created. Fill both from the documented option and keep unknown entries visible. The DigitalOcean daily percentage-based row explicitly lists both seven backups and seven-day retention; that statement applies to that row, not every backup product. A generic retention label is insufficient evidence for the number or timing of recovery points.

## What should I keep before buying?

Keep the selected server configuration, backup option name, source URL, observation date, billing period, currency, tax treatment, and each requirement decision together. Recheck them at checkout. If the option fails a gate, record the failure instead of comparing its price as an equivalent service. If it passes the documentation gates, a separate restoration exercise would still be needed to establish whether your own application can recover as required. We have not performed that exercise, so this page leaves that result unknown.

# VPS server transfer allowance: which traffic actually counts?

A VPS server transfer allowance is meaningful only after checking which traffic the provider meters. In the DigitalOcean Droplet example, public outbound traffic counts toward the team pool, inbound traffic is free, and private VPC traffic follows a different route. IPv6 uses the public interface. Counted transfer is not automatically an extra charge: the applicable allowance still matters. This page maps routing evidence; it does not inspect your traffic or calculate your bill.

## The scope of the official rule

DigitalOcean documents a team-level Droplet transfer pool. Public-interface outbound traffic contributes to it; IPv6 uses that interface. Transfers between Droplets using VPC networking use a private interface. Its documentation also excludes outbound transfer it determines was dropped by a DigitalOcean firewall rule. These are Droplet-specific accounting rules, not universal promises about every VPS or every firewall. Keep the product and network path attached to the evidence.

## Our original route register

We built a register with product, direction, network route, IP version and provider-confirmed firewall-drop evidence. It deliberately does not store an advertised bandwidth speed as a transfer allowance. A product boundary is checked before the routing rules, so an object-storage record cannot silently inherit the Droplet classification. Missing direction or route produces an unresolved label rather than a free label. This makes the register suitable for checking an explanation against its documented scope, without inventing account usage.

## Reproduce the routing cases

All rows are synthetic test inputs, not measured packets, purchased servers or customer invoices.

| Case | Direction | Route | IP version | Classification | 
| A | inbound | public | 4 | inbound_not_counted | 
| B | outbound | public | 4 | counts_team_pool | 
| C | outbound | vpc_private | 4 | vpc_private_not_counted | 
| D | outbound | unknown | 6 | counts_team_pool | 
| E | outbound | public | 4 | provider_dropped_not_counted | 
| F | outbound | unknown | unknown | unresolved_route | 
| G | outbound | vpc_private | 6 | inconsistent_route_evidence | 

[Download inputs and official capture hashes](audit-inputs.json) · [Download the runnable checker](audit-checker.py)

## Cases A and B: the same interface, opposite directions

We supplied two public IPv4 fixtures and changed only direction. Case A is inbound and returns inbound not counted. Case B is outbound and returns counts team pool. This paired test isolates the direction field: a public address alone cannot explain which side of the allowance a transfer belongs to. Neither fixture includes a byte quantity or a team allowance. Consequently, the result identifies an accounting category while leaving monetary cost uncomputed. That is narrower than claiming the transfer caused a bill.

## Case C: private VPC traffic needs a route field

Our third fixture is outbound IPv4 over a private VPC route. Its result is VPC private not counted. The input is an explicit synthetic route, not a conclusion drawn from the destination being another server. A nearby destination or shared provider name cannot fill this field in an actual inventory. Compare this case with public outbound case B to see why a route must remain visible beside direction. We have not configured a VPC or tested packet delivery.

## Cases D and G: IPv6 and contradictory evidence

Case D supplies outbound IPv6 and leaves the route cell unknown. The documented IPv6 public-interface rule makes this case count toward the team pool. Case G instead supplies IPv6 together with a private VPC label; our checker marks that combination inconsistent rather than selecting whichever value looks cheaper. This is a consistency test of our model, not a network diagnosis. The conflicting record must be resolved before using it in a transfer comparison. No IPv6 connection was generated for this audit.

## Case E: keep the firewall exception narrowly labelled

This public outbound fixture sets provider firewall drop evidence true and receives provider dropped not counted. The flag represents DigitalOcean-determined drops in the synthetic case. It does not represent a local application refusing a connection or a user guessing that a packet disappeared. Our register therefore records the authority behind the exception instead of treating every failure as excluded traffic. Removing the flag returns the normal public outbound classification. The test does not claim access to a provider firewall log.

## Case F: unknown routes do not become free transfer

The final unresolved fixture supplies outbound direction while leaving route and IP version unknown. The result remains unresolved route. We also tested a missing direction and obtained unresolved direction, and a Spaces product input produced outside scope. An invalid direction is rejected. These tests protect three separate boundaries: incomplete evidence, a different service and malformed inputs. None can quietly become a zero-cost route. Add actual routing evidence privately before replacing an unresolved cell; the checker has no account connection.

## Does traffic that counts toward the pool always cost extra?

No. A counted category contributes usage to the applicable allowance; it is not proof of an overage. The actual allowance and usage must be known before discussing an extra transfer charge. This route classifier intentionally produces no monetary estimate. A large network-speed number is also a different field from a quantity of included transfer.

## What remains unmeasured

This is a documentation-derived model for DigitalOcean Droplets only. No traffic was generated, no VPS was rented and no account invoice was read. It does not calculate accrued allowances, predict monthly usage or substitute another provider's policies. Documentation can change; preserve the applicable product and evidence date when checking a quote.

# Vultr pricing: what still costs money after stopping or destroying a server?

Stopping a Vultr server does not stop its instance charges. Destroying it ends that instance charge, but a snapshot you keep has a separate storage charge. Check independently retained volumes and reserved IPs as separate items before concluding that your account has no continuing costs. This page audits the boundary between those items; it does not inspect your account or provide a current checkout total.

## Reproducible audit inputs

All four rows below are synthetic software fixtures, not customer accounts or observed bills.

| Case | Instance | Snapshot | Volume | Reserved IP | Result | 
| A | stopped | absent | absent | absent | instance | 
| B | destroyed | present | absent | absent | snapshot | 
| C | destroyed | absent | present | unknown | block_volume, reserved_ip_presence_unknown | 
| D | destroyed | absent | absent | absent | clear within listed scope | 

[Download the inputs, results and evidence hashes](audit-inputs.json) and [the runnable checker](audit-checker.py).

## Does a stopped Vultr instance still cost money?

Yes. The official stopped-instance billing documentation says charges continue while the server remains allocated. Turning it off is not a billing exit. Destroying that instance is a separate action; review retained objects and preserve any data you need before acting. Our lifecycle checker models those separate inventory fields, without accessing your account.

## The documented boundary

Vultr documents hourly server billing from deployment and continued charges while stopped. Its snapshot page separately prices stored snapshots at USD 0.05 per GB per month. Its Block Storage deletion guide says deleting the volume stops further charges and removes its data. Those statements identify different resource lifecycles. They do not establish that destroying a server automatically removes every other resource in an account.

## Audit case A: the server is stopped

We supplied our checker with instance=stopped, snapshot=false, volume=false and ip=false. The result contains instance in the known-billable list, has an empty unresolved list, and does not mark the exit clear. Changing only the power state therefore does not complete our documented exit check. The false values are explicit fixture inputs, not observations of a customer account. This case tests whether a reassuring stopped label can incorrectly override the server billing rule.

## Audit case B: destruction with a saved snapshot

Our second fixture changes instance to destroyed and snapshot to true; volume and ip remain false. The instance category disappears from the result, but snapshot remains known billable. The exit is still not clear. This comparison isolates one retained object rather than claiming an entire bill vanished. Snapshot size is deliberately absent from the fixture, so the checker reports a category without inventing a monetary amount. The published storage unit price alone cannot fill in that missing size.

## Audit case C: a volume remains and the IP is unknown

The third fixture has instance=destroyed, snapshot=false, volume=true and ip=unknown. Its unresolved list contains block_volume and reserved_ip_presence_unknown. We did not give either item a made-up price or infer that it was automatically released. A retained volume needs its own documented deletion and charge check. The IP cell needs an account inventory and applicable terms before it can become present or absent. This case tests the important failure mode where an empty compute list is mistaken for a complete inventory.

## Audit case D: clear within the listed scope

The fourth fixture sets instance=destroyed and all three retained-resource flags to false. Both output lists are empty, so our checker marks only the listed scope clear. That result is narrower than an account-wide zero-cost claim: other services, accrued charges, taxes or resources outside this register have not been inspected. We also tested an unknown snapshot flag separately; it stays unresolved and prevents a clear result. An unsupported instance state is rejected rather than treated as destruction. Download the fixtures to reproduce these checks.

## Use our four-field exit register

Our register separates instance state, retained snapshot presence, retained block-volume presence and reserved-IP presence. Each retained-resource cell accepts present, absent or unknown. This design makes the inventory explicit: an unfilled cell cannot silently mean absent. Our two result lists distinguish documented continuing categories from unresolved checks, so a missing price is not the same as a zero price. Copy this structure for the resources you actually have, add the relevant resource identifiers privately, and verify deletion status before changing a cell. This article has not deleted any resource or accessed a billing console.

## Why can a charge appear after a server is destroyed?

A remaining invoice does not by itself establish new post-destruction instance usage. Vultr says monthly invoices reflect accrued charges from the previous billing period. Review the service, usage period and independently retained objects before interpreting the total. No real invoice was tested here.

## What remains unknown

This audit does not establish account-specific tax, credits, monetary charges for reserved IPs or volumes, automatic release behavior, or a current server quote. Removing resources can delete data; preserve anything you need before acting. The checker is an original, reproducible documentation model, not a live billing tool.

## Official sources

# Windows VPS server: does preinstalled Windows mean the licence cost is included?

No. Preinstalled Windows establishes how a server is delivered; it does not by itself prove that a particular Windows VPS server quote includes the Windows licence cost. Look for an explicit inclusion statement, a separate licence charge, or a documented customer-licence route tied to that offer. If that evidence is missing, record inclusion as unknown rather than adding a guessed fee or treating it as zero.

## What the official documents actually establish

The OVHcloud US Windows VPS page says the operating system is preinstalled. Our captured landing page does not establish licence inclusion for a selected checkout configuration. Separately, Microsoft documents Azure Hybrid Benefit as a conditional route for qualifying existing Windows Server licences, with active Software Assurance or qualifying subscriptions. That Azure-specific rule is not an inclusion promise for OVHcloud or every Windows VPS provider. Neither document reveals this reader's chosen quote or licence inventory.

## Our original licence evidence register

Our register stores the provider, region, plan identifier, Windows edition, licence route, the supporting document and whether its scope matches the selected offer. It keeps installation in a separate field. For our OVHcloud landing-page sample, installation is documented while quote-specific inclusion remains unestablished. We intentionally leave a monetary licence field empty: no selected checkout or separate charge was captured. The register prevents a convenient installation label from filling a price field that the evidence has not supplied.

## Run the evidence fixtures

These six cases are synthetic software inputs, not live provider quotes, customer licences or tested invoices. The checker labels evidence completeness; it does not decide legal eligibility.

| Case | Authored input | Expected evidence label | 
| A | unknown; scope True | unresolved_inclusion | 
| B | included; scope True | included_claim_documented | 
| C | separate; scope True | separate_charge_documented | 
| D | bring_your_own; scope True | unresolved_eligibility | 
| E | included; scope False | unresolved_scope | 
| F | bring_your_own; scope True | customer_license_route_documented | 

[Download fixtures and capture hashes](audit-inputs.json) · [Download the runnable checker](audit-checker.py)

## Case A: the installation-only trap

We entered a matching scope, a true preinstalled flag and an unknown licence mode. The checker returned unresolved inclusion. Changing the installation flag cannot produce an included claim, because that flag is deliberately absent from the inclusion decision. This is a test of our field separation, not an assertion that a particular provider charges extra. The missing statement remains a question to resolve for the actual offer. No amount is calculated from the operating system label.

## Case B: an explicit scoped inclusion claim

Our second fixture supplies included mode and a matching offer scope. The checker returns included claim documented. That label means the synthetic evidence says included for the selected scope; it does not certify the provider, authenticate a licence or guarantee a final payable total. Region, edition and plan identifiers belong beside the statement so it can be checked again. The contrast with case A tests whether explicit evidence, rather than installation alone, changes the result.

## Case C: a separately documented charge

The third input supplies separate mode, matching scope and a true charge evidence flag. Its result is separate charge documented. We also removed the charge evidence in an additional test and obtained unresolved charge. This distinguishes a known charging route from a completed price lookup. Our fixture carries no monetary value, billing period or currency, so the output cannot become a numerical surcharge. A real comparison would still need the provider's applicable amount and unit.

## Cases D and F: customer licences need their own evidence

Both fixtures use customer licence mode and matching scope. Case D leaves eligibility evidence unknown, which returns unresolved eligibility. Case F sets that evidence flag true and returns customer licence route documented. The true flag is invented test data, not a finding about any reader. Microsoft's documented prerequisites motivate keeping this field separate. We do not infer eligibility from possession of an installation image, a product key or the ability to boot Windows.

## Case E: evidence for a different scope

This fixture supplies an included statement but marks scope matching false. The checker returns unresolved scope before inspecting the charging mode. A statement attached to another plan, region or edition therefore cannot clear our register for the intended offer. We separately tested a missing scope flag and got the same unresolved result. This conservative ordering makes the evidence reference useful: it must identify what the claim covers, rather than merely proving that some Windows offer exists.

## Does unknown mean that the Windows licence costs extra?

No. Unknown means the collected evidence has not established inclusion or a separate charge for the selected quote. It is not a zero, an extra fee or proof of invalid licensing. Request an offer-specific statement before relying on the comparison. A customer-provided licence route also needs its own documented eligibility check; installation alone answers neither question.

## What this audit has not tested

No server was rented, no licence was purchased and no billing account or checkout was accessed. The checker is a reproducible evidence model, not a live billing tool or a legal licensing assessment. Final tax, credits, selected configuration prices and reader-specific rights remain outside this audit. The synthetic cases should not be presented as provider offers.

# Privacy Policy

Last updated: 2026-10-09

## Overview

This privacy policy explains what information vpspricewatch.com collects and how it is used. By using the site you agree to the practices described here.

## Advertising and affiliate links

This site participates in affiliate marketing. Some outbound links to hosting providers are affiliate links issued and tracked through the Admitad affiliate network (admitad.com). If you follow one of these links and later make a qualifying purchase, this site may earn a commission.

No extra cost to you: affiliate links do not change the price you pay. Prices shown on this site are observations taken from official provider pages, and the final price and terms must always be confirmed with the provider.

Current sponsored partners: is*hosting, HyperHost, Godlike.Host and ProHoster. Sponsored placements for these partners appear on the homepage and the provider comparison page. The list of partners may change as partnerships are added or removed; this page reflects the current state.

How sponsored links are marked: sponsored placements are labelled Sponsored and their links carry rel="nofollow sponsored" so that search engines can identify them as paid placements. Sponsored content is always shown separately from price observations.

Editorial independence: affiliate commissions do not change how we report prices, rankings, or comparisons. This site does not sell hosting itself and cannot change provider prices, accounts, or billing.

When you follow an affiliate link you leave this site. The affiliate network and the advertiser may then process referral information under their own privacy policies, which we do not control.

## Data we use

When you visit, the following data may be processed:

- Server and CDN logs: the hosting provider (Cloudflare) records request metadata such as IP address, browser type, requested URL, and timestamp for security and performance.
- Analytics: privacy-respecting, aggregated usage statistics may be collected to understand which pages are useful. Cloudflare Web Analytics is enabled by the hosting service and collects performance and usage measurements. No Google Analytics measurement script is currently installed in the site source.
- Affiliate attribution: following a sponsored link sends you to the affiliate network, which may set a cookie or use similar technologies to record the referral (referring page, time, and a network identifier) so that a resulting purchase can be attributed. This site only receives aggregated statistics, never your payment or personal details.
- Advertising cookies: if and when additional ad networks are enabled, those networks may set cookies to measure impressions and serve relevant ads.
- Email: if you contact us by email, we store the message and address only to reply.

## Your choices

You can disable or block cookies in your browser, including third-party cookies. Blocking them prevents affiliate referral attribution and ad personalization but will not affect access to any core content on this site. For ad personalization controls, use the opt-out tools provided by the advertising network or by Admitad.

## Contact

See the [contact page](https://vpspricewatch.com/contact) for the current availability of a contact channel.
